etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French scene, from Latin scaena, scēna, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene, stage”). Doublet of scena and skene.

definitions.definition: The location of an event that attracts attention.
(theater) The decorations; furnishings and backgrounds of a stage, representing the place in which the action of a play is set.
(theater, film, television, radio) A part of a dramatic work that is set in the same place or time. In the theatre, generally a number of scenes constitute an act.

quote.citation: 1904–1905, Baroness Orczy [i.e., Emma Orczy], “The Affair at the Novelty Theatre”, in The Case of Miss Elliott, London: T[homas] Fisher Unwin, published 1905, →OCLC; republished as popular edition, London: Greening & Co., 1909, OCLC 11192831, quoted in The Case of Miss Elliott (ebook no. 2000141h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg of Australia, February 2020:
quote.text: Miss Phyllis Morgan, as the hapless heroine dressed in the shabbiest of clothes, appears in the midst of a gay and giddy throng; she apostrophises all and sundry there, including the villain, and has a magnificent scene which always brings down the house, and nightly adds to her histrionic laurels.

definitions.definition: The location, time, circumstances, etc., in which something occurs, or in which the action of a story, play, or the like, is set up.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene prologue]:
quote.text: In Troy, there lies the scene.

quote.citation: c. 1810, John M. Mason, On Religious Controversy:
quote.text: The world is a vast scene of strife.

definitions.definition: A combination of objects or events in view or happening at a given moment at a particular place.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene v, page 1:
quote.text: Through what new scenes and changes must we pass!

definitions.definition: A landscape, or part of a landscape; scenery.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Palamon and Arcite”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A sylvan scene with various greens was drawn, / Shades on the sides, and in the midst a lawn.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “Foreword”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: He turned back to the scene before him and the enormous new block of council dwellings. The design was some way after Corbusier but the block was built up on plinths and resembled an Atlantic liner swimming diagonally across the site.

definitions.definition: An exhibition of passionate or strong feeling before others, creating embarrassment or disruption; often, an artificial or affected action, or course of action, done for effect; a theatrical display.

quote.text: Probably no lover of scenes would have had very long to wait or some explosions between parties, both equally ready to take offence, and careless of giving it.

definitions.definition: An element of fiction writing. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
A social environment consisting of an informal, vague group of people with a uniting interest; their sphere of activity; a subculture.
A youth subculture popular in the Anglosphere in the 2000s and early 2010s.     Scene (subculture) on Wikipedia
(BDSM) A BDSM fantasy that is acted out.
(transitive) To exhibit as a scene; to make a scene of; to display.
